In the first quarter of 2026, the Rosenbauer Group continued its growth trajectory and generated revenues of €303.8 million (1–3/2025: €263.6 million), an increase of 15.3% compared with the same period of the previous year. This was due in particular to the higher number of vehicle deliveries and improved business volume in the areas of equipment, service, and Preventive Fire Protection. With growth of 16.8%, the Vehicles product segment recorded the strongest increase. 
The higher business volume and improved contribution margins for vehicles delivered led to a significant increase in the operating result. EBITDA rose to €23.0 million (1–3/2025: €16.7 million) and EBIT amounted to €14.4 million (1–3/2025: €9.0 million). At the end of the reporting period, the Group’s EBT reached a pleasing €10.4 million (1–3/2025: €1.8 million) and net profit was €9.4 million, considerably higher than the previous year’s figure (1–3/2025: €0.1 million).
“The significant improvement in EBIT, EBT, and net profit in the first quarter underscores the current high demand and the increasing number of vehicle deliveries in the firefighting business. At the same time, the continued high order backlog – which exceeds our annual turnover – demonstrates persistently strong market demand and gives us a good basis for planning future business development,” said Robert Ottel, CEO of Rosenbauer International AG.
Revenues and result of operations
Revenues in the first quarter of 2026 stood at €303.8 million (1–3/2025: €263.6 million). Consolidated revenues were spread across the different sales regions as follows: Europe area 50%, Americas area 31%, Asia-Pacific area 9%, Middle East & Africa area 8%, and the Preventive Fire Protection segment 2%.
From January to March 2026, the Rosenbauer Group recorded another pleasing order intake of €342.9 million (1–3/2025: €358.7 million), which exceeded the revenues of €303.8 million achieved in the same period. The Europe area and the Preventive Fire Protection (PFP) segment succeeded in boosting their order intake, while orders in the Americas area remained roughly at the same level as the previous year. Incoming orders in the Middle East & Africa and Asia-Pacific areas were lower than the previous year’s figure. 
The order backlog remained almost unchanged at €2,348.3 million at the end of the first quarter of 2026 (March 31, 2025: €2,343.5 million). With this order book, the Rosenbauer Group has a solid basis for further profitable revenue growth.
Financial and net assets position
Net debt increased to €301.1 million from the previous year’s figure of €288.0 million. The main driver of this was the increase in trade working capital to €557.1 million (1–3/2025: €464.7 million), which involved additional financing requirements. The equity ratio, however, improved to 27.0% (Q1–Q3 2025: 25.2%).
At €-41.4 million (1–3/2025: €-6.8 million), cash flow from operating activities remained negative in the first quarter due to the increase in production and the associated higher trade working capital. Cash flow is therefore negatively impacted in the short term due to growth. However, positive cash flow from operating activities is expected for 2026 as a whole.
Outlook
Sector development is stable at the start of 2026. Well-filled order books and stabilized supply chains are supporting both production and delivery and providing a solid basis for positive revenue development over the course of the year. At the same time there are uncertainties, particularly with regard to public investment budgets, trade policy and geopolitical tensions in the Middle East.
The Group’s Executive Board thus expects sales and earnings to increase further in 2026 and anticipates revenues of around €1.6 billion. Taking existing uncertainties into account, the EBIT margin is expected to continue to improve to over 6%.

E-Mobility
The answer is electric. Find out why the future at Rosenbauer is electrified.
Learn more
The future is electric
Moving solutions thanks to alternative drive concepts
A rethink is taking place. In politics, cooperation, a wide variety of industries – indeed, in each and every individual. As market leaders, we see it as our responsibility not only to support this positive trend, but to expand it. That's why Rosenbauer is making a sustainable contribution to the fire service industry: with battery-powered electric drive concepts. We see the future in “e-mobility” as a synonym for alternative drive concepts.
With innovative technologies we are actively shaping change and setting new standards for firefighting operation. Our electric drive concepts enable both driving and firefighting operations without propulsion-related exhaust emissions, as long as the vehicle is powered exclusively by the battery.
the panther electric
A new era begins
Electrifying developments for the future
Our products
Our target as market leader is to develop the most effective and future-proof system solutions for the fire service industry. Through the consistent electrification of our fire engines and equipment, we are ready for tomorrow today. Even if energy supply continues to evolve, hybrid technologies will emerge that rely on an electric drive architecture.
Image: red RT on stage with blue lighting
A milestone in firefighting.
Image: Black PANTHER electric on stage with blue lighting
## PANTHER electric
A new era begins.
L32A-Xs electric against a blue background
## L32A-XS electric
The World Innovation

Customer Stories
Skip slider
RT on the new bridge in Linz
E-mobility thought through from A to Z
A groundbreaking idea, born long before politics, media and society not just suggested but demanded a change in thinking. Rosenbauer has always been a trailblazer, an innovator and an outside-the-box thinker in disaster protection.
Read more (Opens in new tab)
Side view of the Vancouver Fire Department's RTX
Endurance test in Canada
On paper, the RTX's features look impressive. In Vancouver, the city of contrasts, the emergency vehicle has to prove itself. Canada's eighth largest city presents him with countless challenges.
Read more (Opens in new tab)
Close-up: two fire engines of the BF Basel
Grüezi in Switzerland
Basel-city, the canton in northwestern Switzerland bordering France and Germany, has earned this title. The first fully electric police cars were purchased in 2019. And other authorities are also turning to electric drive.
Read more (Opens in new tab)
RT on the street in front of several houses
Why e-mobility in the firefighting industry?
We did not take the decision lightly. It was based on a number of factors that took both ecological and economic aspects into account. Here we would like to show why Rosenbauer considers e-mobility to be the right technology for the future of the firefighting industry.
Read more (Opens in new tab)
Front view of the RT on a road in a rural area at full speed.
Immediate impact in action
Firefighters worldwide literally walk through fire for us every day. They are there when we need them. And Rosenbauer is there for these people. Always striving to make operations even safer and more efficient.
Read more (Opens in new tab)
RT vehicle at sunset
Changing today for tomorrow
Low-noise and locally emission-free – these are the obvious benefits our innovative drive concept has. But the implications reach much further. Locally, globally, and also in people's minds, something is being ignited. Something of central importance for the future.
Read more (Opens in new tab)
Detailed view of the RT electric 
Investing in the future. Benefiting in the long term.
Let's take the future into our own hands. Guided by sustainable technology that shows us the right path. We continuously refine and develop it further, while boldly moving ahead. The PANTHER electric already demonstrates how innovative drive concepts can combine sustainable mobility with full operational capability: driving and pumping functions can be powered entirely by batteries, while a diesel backup system ensures maximum reliability whenever additional energy is required. Join us on this journey toward a future that is both sustainable and secure.
Read more (Opens in new tab)
Service employee working in front of a laptop
Intelligent Services. Unbound Readiness.
Rosenbauer not only responds to the challenges of today's world in the development of alternative drive concepts. The customer service is being adjusted accordingly.
Read more (Opens in new tab)
Front view of the RT in the open air
Efficiency, measured by the degree of efficiency
A groundbreaking idea, born long before politics, media and society not just suggested but demanded a change in thinking. Rosenbauer has always been a trailblazer, an innovator and an outside-the-box thinker in disaster protection.
Read more (Opens in new tab)
Rosenbauer lettering on the office building at sunset
Living sustainability in society
E-mobility promotes sustainability through lower emissions and greater resource conservation. Rosenbauer uses this technology to develop more environmentally friendly and efficient emergency vehicles. For example, in the PANTHER electric, driving and pumping functions can be operated using battery-electric power. A diesel backup system is available to provide additional energy when needed.
Read more (Opens in new tab)
Side view of the yellow PANTHER electric at Dallas Airport
Dallas Love Field Airport
Dallas Love Field is making history: In 2025, the airport will be the first in the world to put the all-electric PANTHER 6x6 electric into operation. This is made possible by a groundbreaking partnership between Rosenbauer America and the Dallas fire service, who are jointly developing the innovative aircraft rescue & fire fighting vehicle until it is ready for series production.
Read more (Opens in new tab)
Jump to slider start

The future is electric
Energy- & Charging Infrastructure
Climate change is a reality, and a manmade one at that. Global temperatures are rising, and extreme weather events are increasing. The consequences are noticeable: floods, heat waves, and power outages, which also endanger critical infrastructure such as fire stations.
This means that infrastructure must not only be climate-friendly, but also resilient. Climate adaptation is just as important as climate protection. A resilient energy and mobility infrastructure protects against failures and ensures operational readiness, even in times of crisis. These necessary steps can be achieved through the energy and mobility transition.
Learn more
the answer is electric
Our path to electromobility
Skip slider
The RT: An idea becomes reality
The journey begins
In 2011, the first considerations about alternative drive concepts were voiced. We address future challenges and develop scenarios in a wide range of areas. The foundations for the RT and the trend map are laid.
Graphic of the Fire Department Trendmap 5.0
The RT: An idea becomes reality
The Concept Fire Truck
In 2016, the CFT will be presented as chassis of the 150th anniversary celebrations. The idea of e-mobility in firefighting thus becomes tangible and can be experienced.
Concept Fire Truck in front of modern building
The RT: An idea becomes reality
The launch event
In 2020 the time has come: The RT will be officially presented in Linz. The event is a complete success. Positive feedback and awards for the RT confirm the path we have chosen.
RT on stage at the launch event
The RT: An idea becomes reality
Convincing test phase
The RT is undergoing a 13-month test phase with the Berlin Fire Department. The result: round bar 1,400 deployments, on busy days up to 16 times within 24 hours, without fault and usually without intermediate charging. Over 90% of all operations could be completed purely electrically. The RT is taken over into regular operation.
Close-up of the Rosenbauer logo on the RT
The RT: An idea becomes reality
RTX goes America
The first RTX (RT in US design) will be delivered in 2022. In a short test phase, over 98% of all operations could be carried out electrically. And since September 2022, the RTX has been portion of the regular vehicle fleet in Los Angeles City.
Three RTX side by side on the FDIC
10 Years of Technology Development - World Premiere at Interschutz
The Rosenbauer Electric Line-Up
The Rosenbauer E-Lineup will celebrate its premiere at Interschutz 2022. The fully electric PANTHER electric combines maximum performance with sustainable technology and enables multiple uses on a single charge. The RT revolutionizes municipal firefighting operation with its compact, maneuverable construction and a fully integrated cabin for optimal ergonomics and safety.
Rosenbauer electric lineup at Interschutz
Proven functionalities. Future-oriented technology.
The PANTHER electric
Available to order since 2024: The PANTHER electric combines proven wattage with future-oriented technology. Thanks to the fully electric drive and Energy Backup System, multiple uses per charge are possible – without compromising on speed, wattage and safety.
PANTHER electric on runway
Jump to slider start
Advantages of new technologies
E-mobility in firefighting technology
Three firefighters discuss in the cockpit of the RT
Noise reduction
Electric vehicles are very quiet. This leads to less noise pollution in cities and residential areas, which improves the quality of life of residents. Less noise also means that emergency services can react more attentively and quickly in emergency situations.
Red RT driving on a bridge
No local emissions
In purely battery-electric operation, no propulsion-related exhaust emissions are generated. If the diesel-powered backup system is used, exhaust emissions are produced. This is particularly beneficial in urban areas where air quality is often a major problem.
Close-up of a side Rosenbauer logo on an RT
Alternative uses
Another advantage of e-mobility is the possibility of bidirectional use, such as Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G). This technology enables electric vehicles not only to draw energy from the grid but also to feed excess energy back into the grid. This contributes to the stabilization of the electricity grid and promotes the integration of renewable energies.
Frontal shot: RT at sunset in a wide snowy landscape
Longer service intervals
Electric drives require little maintenance. The long service life and high availability of individual components is also reflected in longer service intervals. Electric motors are simpler and more compact. Fewer installed parts mean less vibration. This makes these engines quieter in operation and also contributes to their durability .
Close-up of an electric logo
Sustainability has many faces
Sustainable technology
The simple superstructure of an electric motor compared to conventional motors makes it more efficient. Another advantage of fewer moving parts: the unit is less susceptible to possible functional problems.
RT drives on snow curves at dusk
The strenght is to be found in serenity
Reliable powerhouse
The electric motors accelerate linearly with little energy loss – meaning they transfer power to the road even on steep climbs. Indispensable when every second counts. In addition, the batteries can be used to operate external consumers on site. If the energy supply runs low, the Energy Backup System guarantees smooth process operation drainage .
Two firefighters in GAROS G10 protective suits extinguish a vegetation fire
## Wildfire
Detect. Act. Extinguish.
Two firefighters in contaminated PPE
## Operational hygiene
Stay clean and healthy.
Section of the trend map

BUSINESS DEVELOPMENT AND THE ECONOMIC SITUATION 1.1. Economic background Up until the first quarter of 2026, the global economy was experiencing an upturn that, whilst not particularly dynamic, was nonetheless robust. The AI-driven technology boom more than offset the dampening effect of the more restrictive US tariff policy; inflation rates were well on the way back to the central banks’ targets, and the central banks were able to ease their monetary policy slightly once again. The outbreak of war in the Middle East and the resulting surge in crude oil prices brought these positive trends to an abrupt halt. Subsequently, economic growth forecasts were revised downwards on several occasions, whilst inflation forecasts were revised upwards – in many cases significantly. The uncertainty surround-ing the duration of the situation and whether it would escalate further or stabilise was so great that economic research institutes began – in addition to their usual practice of presenting a medium-range baseline scenario – to set out several models with considerable ranges in terms of GDP growth and inflation. The baseline scenario was, for the most part, the one that assumed a peace agreement would be reached in the near future, the Strait of Hormuz would be reopened swiftly, and this would lead to a return to more moderate prices and an adequate supply of crude oil and petroleum products. With concrete peace negotiations between the US and Iran having begun in mid-June 2026, this baseline scenario therefore appears to be coming to fruition. Crude oil price volatility is back under control for the time being, uncertainties have eased somewhat, long-term damage is within manageable limits, and it is therefore becoming increasingly likely that the eco-nomic forecasts drawn up on the basis of these assumptions will be borne out. Nevertheless, the sharp downturn in the spring of 2026 marks a turning point in the overall trend: according to the OECD’s forecast of early June 2026, global economic growth for 2026 as a whole is expected to be just 2.8%, down from 3.4% the previous year. Despite the significant rise in global uncertainty and the general sharp increase in the price of crude oil following the outbreak of the war in Iran, economies were affected to varying degrees by the negative consequences. Whilst the impact on the countries in the Middle East directly affected by the conflict was considerable, simply due to the damage caused by the war, many emerging economies in Asia and Latin America appeared relatively unscathed. In the US, the economic slowdown was once again significantly less severe than in Europe. At the turn of the year 2025/26, GDP growth forecasts for the US for the current year 2026 stood at around 2%, whilst inflation forecasts for 2026 were just under 3%. In the case of the former, there were hardly any changes; they remained at around 2% both before the outbreak of the war and after peace negotiations began. Inflation forecasts, on the other hand, were also revised significantly upwards for the US following the outbreak of the war, in some cases by just under 1 percentage point. This has put expectations regarding key interest rates for 2026 into perspective: rather than expecting rate cuts, the consensus is now that policy will remain slightly restrictive for the time being, meaning that key interest rates will stay unchanged. MATERIAL RISKS AND UNCERTAINTIES The long-term success of Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich Group is largely dependent upon active risk management. In order to achieve this target, Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich, as the dominant group company, has implemented risk management with structures that facilitate the identification and measurement of all risks in the Group in accordance with sections 39, 39a, Austrian Banking Act and the Credit Institution Risk Management Regulation (KI-RMV) (credit risks, equity risks, liquidity risks, market risks, macroeconomic risks, operational risks and other risks) and their active managerial counteraction. Credit, investment and operational risk are managed by RMKM (Risk Management Credit, Reporting, Op-erational Risk), while liquidity, market and macroeconomic risk are managed by RMIM (Risk Management ICAAP & Market Risk). ESG (environment, social, governance) risks, as the latest dimension of risks, were integrated into the existing risk categories, with the greatest focus remaining on climate and environmental risks – in part because social and governance risks have not been classified as material. The overall risk strategy approved by the Managing Board ensures that the risks assumed by the Bank are consistent with the corporate strategy. The Managing Board and the Supervisory Board are regularly given reports about the risk situation. For more detailed information on the overall financial risks in the Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich Group in the first half of 2026 and the objectives and methods of risk management, please refer to Note “7. Risk report” in the notes to the consolidated financial statements. Macroeconomic influences and credit risk developments A year ago, this section anticipated a marked economic recovery, but while this still appears to be under way, it now looks set to be significantly slower and weaker than hoped – not least because of the Iran conflict. The ECB’s interest rate rises, both those that have already taken place and those still expected this year, are dampening an already very weak appetite for investment. In the first half of 2026, credit risk – when considering only specific allowances and provisions – was approximately on a par with the corresponding period of the previous year. The positive impact of the release of portfolio provisions was less pronounced than in the first half of 2025, particularly as ongoing conflicts, lacklustre expenditure-side budgetary measures and rising interest rates are weighing on economic prospects. Insolvency figures amongst corporate clients in the key markets of Austria and Southern Germany remain high, and further difficulties are to be expected given the bleak outlook for German car manufacturers, particularly as many suppliers in these key regions are directly or indirectly dependent on them. Despite the decidedly adverse circumstances, the Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich Group has managed to keep its NPL ratio well below 6%, and a further decrease below the 5% mark is forecast for the end of 2026, particularly as a number of larger non-performing real estate loans are on the verge of being realised or returning to performing status. An application has now been submitted to the ECB, with effect from 29 May 2026, to apply the Internal Ratings-Based Approach (IRB Approach) to all corporate customer financing at Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich. This results in risk-adequate capital requirements – put simply, loans to customers with top credit ratings require less capital to underpin them than loans to companies with weaker credit ratings. Once this application has been approved, it should therefore be pos-sible to offer significantly more competitive financing terms, particularly to customers with a strong credit rating, which will lead to a further improvement in portfolio quality in the medium term. Another side effect of the approval would be an increase in the already substantial capital buffer. In addition to the analysis of customs duties carried out last year, efforts were also made in the first half of 2026, in consultation with the customers affected, to quantify the impact of the war in Iran on the portfolio. The results show that the effects have so far been fairly manageable for the vast majority of customers. However, the consequences of a pro-longed blockade of the Strait of Hormuz and the resulting sustained rise in oil and gas prices would act as further brakes on economic growth and would likely cause corporate default rates to rise even further. OUTLOOK Building on its solid capital base, its high level of financial stability and its sustained successful growth trajectory, Raiff-eisenlandesbank Oberösterreich aims to further strengthen its strong market position in the Austrian banking sector. With its “IMPULS 2030” strategy, Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich has developed a clear roadmap for the future, and the associated initiatives are being implemented on an ongoing basis. One key objective in this regard is to consistently consolidate and expand its position as a leading corporate bank. The focus is on entrepreneurial thinking and action, customer focus and the consistent further development of the business model. Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich con-tinues to tailor its activities to clearly defined customer segments and focuses on bespoke solutions, excellent advisory services and the swift resolution of customer enquiries. An efficient, modular and market-oriented operating model supplies the necessary foundation. Through close cooperation with businesses, institutions and partners, as well as through its strong network of equity in-vestments, Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich is driving economic development in its home market. A strong focus lies on the continued digitalisation and data-driven management of customer business. This involves developing a compre-hensive customer profile that brings together information on risk, needs and returns and is supplemented by modern CRM solutions. Clear standards, data-driven activity management and hybrid support models that combine personal contact with digital and scalable service approaches strengthen sales performance in the long term. Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich is working to further develop its range of products and services in line with its stra-tegic priorities. These include, in particular, the expansion of ESG-focused solutions, the further development of interna-tional business and the expansion of payment services and other services. Through close cooperation within the Austrian Raiffeisen sector and with specialist partners, the Bank aims to create added value in selected business areas and expand its range of services. Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich is already making targeted use of the potential offered by artificial intelligence to further develop its business and operational processes and will continue to step up these efforts in the future. By develop-ing its own AI strategy, the Bank has laid the groundwork for systematically identifying areas of application and embedding AI in a sustainable manner across relevant areas. The focus is on improving efficiency and data quality, supporting data-driven decision-making and further enhancing customer service and sales. Furthermore, the use of AI helps to identify and manage risks at an early stage while also supporting the analysis and creation of digital content. Artificial intelligence thus makes a significant contribution to achieving the Bank’s strategic objectives and to strengthening its long-term viability. In addition to traditional loan financing, Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich will continue to prioritise the provision of equity capital as a key component of its range of services. The equity investment companies are not merely providers of capital; they also work alongside businesses as active partners, drawing on their extensive expertise in areas such as corporate development, management accounting, liquidity management, transformation and restructuring. Furthermore, Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich relies on forward-looking liquidity management, comprehensive risk management and consistently data-driven corporate management. Through the ongoing development of processes, digital capabilities and technological solutions, the Bank is laying the foundations to continue strengthening the trust of its cus-tomers in the future. This ensures that it remains a reliable partner for businesses, institutions and private customers and enables it to provide comprehensive support for their investment, growth and future projects. Companies Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich Aktiengesellschaft acts as a regional central institution of the Raiffeisen Banking Group Upper Austria and is recorded in the Commercial Register at the District Court in Linz under the number FN247579m. With Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich AG, the Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich Group includes Austria’s largest regional bank, which pursues the business model of a universal bank, and also has a broad equity in-vestment portfolio. The registered co-operative society RBG OÖ Verbund eGen held 98.92% of the ordinary shares in Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich as at 30 June 2026. RLB Holding eGen Oberösterreich owns 1.08% of the ordinary shares in Raiffeisen-landesbank Oberösterreich. As at 30 June 2026, RBG OÖ Verbund eGen holds more than 50% of the shares in RLB Holding eGen OÖ and represents the ultimate parent company of the Group. The Upper Austrian Raiffeisen banks make up the most important owner groups of the two co-operatives. Both of these are supported by Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich in its function as Upper Austrian headquarters in all banking matters. Since the 2007 financial year, Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich as the highest-level bank in the Group has been subject to the mandatory requirement specified in IAS Regulation (EC) 1606/2002 to prepare consolidated financial state-ments in accordance with the International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) as adopted by the EU. In addition, dis-closures are required in accordance with the regulations of the Austrian Banking Act and the Austrian Commercial Code. This condensed interim financial statement as at 30 June 2026 is in accordance with IAS 34. 1.2. Principles underlying the consolidated financial statements These interim consolidated financial statements comprise the parent company, Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich Ak-tiengesellschaft, and its consolidated subsidiaries (together referred to as the “Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich Group”). The interim consolidated financial statements as at 30 June 2026 have not been subjected to a complete audit, nor have they been inspected by a statutory auditor. Unless noted otherwise, the figures in these financial statements are stated in thousands of euros. Minor discrepancies may arise in calculations because of rounding in the individual items in the financial statements. These interim consolidated financial statements are presented in euros, reflecting the functional currency of the company. Financial statements of fully consolidated companies whose functional currency differs from the group currency are trans-lated into euros employing the modified period-end exchange rate method in accordance with IAS 21. Equity is translated at historical rates while all other assets and equity and liabilities are translated using the relevant period-end exchange rates (middle rates of the European Central Bank (ECB) at the Group reporting date). The items on the income statement are translated using the average foreign currency exchange rates of the ECB. Currency differences resulting from the translation of the equity components using historical rates and the translation of the income statement using average rates compared to the translation using rates prevailing on the reporting date are recognised in the statement of comprehensive income with no effect on the income statement. In these interim consolidated financial statements as at 30 June 2026, the following updates are especially significant given the current risk environment and the economic developments in the first half of 2026. Company valuations Company valuations are required both in order to determine the fair value of investments or investment instruments meas-ured at fair value as well as for impairment tests for investments accounted for using the equity method and goodwill. The main uncertainties in the first half of 2026 stemmed from the geopolitical situation, in particular the ongoing uncertain-ties surrounding trade policy and the impact of the Middle East conflict on the markets and sectors affected. The slight upward trend in economic output in Austria, which had already become apparent in 2025, continued into the start of 2026. Gross domestic product grew by 0.2% in the first quarter of 2026 compared to the fourth quarter of 2025. Industrial activity in Austria and Germany remained subdued in the first half of 2026. New orders continued to be affected by geopolitical uncertainties and rising energy costs. Given the already subdued propensity to invest, the ECB’s interest rate rise in June 2026 – prompted by rising inflationary pressures – is likely to reinforce companies’ cautious approach to investment, their focus on efficiency and their heightened cost discipline. The special fund for infrastructure and climate neutrality in Ger-many is in turn expected to constitute a driving force when it comes to investment activity. The residential property market in Austria and Germany is currently undergoing a moderate recovery. The market envi-ronment in the commercial property sector remains challenging in light of the weak industrial economy and reluctance to invest. Companies actively incorporate ESG-related risks into their strategic and operational planning, particularly in the context of CSRD, the EU Taxonomy and other EU regulatory frameworks, while risks already embedded in the business model are not disclosed separately. Each of the factors mentioned were analysed individually for each company and, where material, reflected in the cash flows underlying the valuation. Double counting of uncertainties in both cash flows and interest rates was avoided. Potential medium- to long-term impairments are evaluated through continuous risk analysis. Valuation of the expected credit loss The impairment provisions of IFRS 9 are based on an expected loss model. Several important discretionary decisions are required for measuring expected credit loss, such as: defining criteria for a significant increase in the credit risk, selecting suitable models and assumptions, defining the number and relative weighting of future-oriented scenarios, defining groups of similar financial assets. The tentative economic recovery is being shaped by the impact of the war in the Middle East. Austria’s economy is particularly feeling the effects of the sharp rise in crude oil prices, which – following a positive start to the year – will lead to a noticeable slowdown in growth in the second half of the year. The OeNB identifies the required fiscal consolidation as another factor restraining growth. Despite considerable consolidation, the budget balance is improving only marginally and is being offset by proac-tive measures (such as reducing ancillary wage costs). Austrian HCPI inflation is expected to remain at 3.6% in 2025, remaining above the ECB’s medium-term target of 2%. Owing to a further energy price shock resulting from the war in the Middle East, the OeNB forecasts an annual HCPI growth rate of 3.2% for 2026. It is only in the following two years that the figure will move closer to the ECB’s medium-term target of 2.4% (2027) and 2.1% (2028). Gross domestic product is projected to grow at 1.1% and 1.2% for 2027 and 2028 respectively, with the rates therefore expected to be slightly above potential growth overall, according to the OeNB. However, this gradual acceleration in economic growth is underpinned by commodity prices returning to normal levels. Following a rise in unemployment in 2024 and 2025, the labour market is currently proving resilient in the face of the current economic climate. According to Eurostat, the unemployment rate is set to remain at 5.7% in 2026 – a level comparable to that of the previous year – and is expected to fall slightly in subsequent years. Companies accounted for using the equity method For investments accounted for using the equity method, where there are indications of impairment or, possibly, a later reversal of impairment: a value in use is determined in addition to the fair value (less sales costs) in accordance with IAS 36 on the basis of corporate planning in order to determine the recoverable amount. IN EUR THOUSAND 30 June 2026 31 Dec. 2025 banks 2,516,189 1,971,540 Non-banks 1,207,206 1,126,986 Companies accounted for using the equity method 3,723,395 3,098,526 Raiffeisen Bank International AG The share of Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich Group in the Raiffeisen Bank International (RBI) Group, amounting to approx. 9.5% (31 December 2025: approx. 9.5%), is reported under credit institutions accounted for using the equity method. RBI is the central institution in the Raiffeisen Banking Group Austria and considers Austria, together with Central and Eastern Europe (CEE), to be its home market. In Austria, the RBI is a leading corporate and investment bank and forms part of the largest banking group in the country. In Central and Eastern Europe (CEE), the RBI acts as a universal bank via its subsidiary banks and is one of the largest financial services providers in the region. Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich Group exerts a significant influence on this investment because the Chief Executive Officer of Raiffeisen-landesbank Oberösterreich, Reinhard Schwendtbauer, is a member of the RBI Supervisory Board and as Deputy Chair-man of the Supervisory Board is an active participant in the strategic decisions made. The impact of Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine remained a key challenge for RBI in the first half of 2026. Potential transactions that could lead to the deconsolidation of the Russian entity were thoroughly reviewed and monitored. RBI has significantly scaled back its operations in Russia since the start of the war and has implemented extensive measures aimed at minimising the risks associated with tougher sanctions and compliance requirements. Efforts continued in the first half of 2026 aimed at ensuring a reduction in business with Russia in line with the ECB’s guidelines. The volume of lending in local currency has fallen by 80% since the start of the war. In September 2024, a Russian court issued a temporary injunction restricting the disposal of all shares in AO Raiffeisen-bank (Network Bank Russia) with immediate effect. A transfer of the shares in AO Raiffeisenbank was not possible as a result of this decision. The decision is related to the legal proceedings initiated by Rasperia Trading Limited (“Rasperia”) against STRABAG SE, its Austrian core shareholders and AO Raiffeisenbank. Taking into account expected compensa-tion claims, AO Raiffeisenbank recognised a provision of EUR 840 million in the fourth quarter of 2024, which was reflected in this amount in RBI’s consolidated financial statements. In January 2025, a Russian court ruled that STRABAG SE and its Austrian core shareholders must pay EUR 2,044 million to Rasperia and that the judgement can be enforced against assets of AO Raiffeisenbank. In April 2025, the Russian central bank executed a judgement in favour of Rasperia in the amount of EUR 1,870 million. EUR 239 million in accrued interest was enforced in May 2025 and a further EUR 0.4 million in July 2025. In June 2025, Rasperia filed an application with the Russian court for an anti-suit injunction involving RBI. Due to the adjusted risk assessment by the RBI Managing Board, AO Raiffeisenbank recognised the expected proceeds from the enforcement of claims against Rasperia in the amount of EUR 1,204 million in the second quarter of 2025. In August 2025, a Russian court lifted the restriction on the disposal of the shares in AO Raiffeisenbank on the grounds that the payment of damages also meant that there was no longer any reason to prohibit the sale. AO Raiffeisenbank subse-quently faced a further claim for damages brought by Rasperia. A provision of EUR 339 million was set aside in the fourth quarter of 2025 following the court’s ruling. EUR 326 million (corresponding to the damages awarded, excluding interest) was enforced in March 2026 by the Russian Central Bank in favour of Rasperia. RBI announced on 23 July 2026 that, in full compliance with EU sanctions law, it had filed a claim in Austria against Rasperia for approx. EUR 3.15 billion in order to obtain damages and to enforce a judgement against Rasperia’s assets in Austria, the latter to take place once Rasperia’s frozen Austrian assets have been released. These assets, which have been frozen as a result of EU sanctions, consist of 28.5 million STRABAG shares, as well as dividends for the financial years from 2021 onwards and a cash distribution arising from STRABAG’s capital reduction in March 2024. AO Raiffeisen-bank will be the second claimant in the Austrian proceedings. The lawsuit was brought on 30 July 2026. Interim Financial Report 2026 58 The Group Interim Financial Report 2026 | Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements 58 RBI recorded a consolidated profit of EUR 1,256 million in the first half of 2026, which was significantly higher by around EUR 1,108 million than the figure for the first half of 2025, which had been burdened by the write-off of the expected proceeds from the enforcement of RBI’s claims against Rasperia’s Austrian assets, amounting to EUR 1,269 million by AO Raiffeisenbank in Russia. In comparison, the consolidated profit excluding Russia in the first half of 2026 totalled EUR 708 million (first half of 2025: EUR 567 million). Net interest income fell year-on-year from EUR 2,972 million to EUR 2,967 million, with the impact of interest rate cuts in Russia being largely offset by rising business volumes in other countries. Despite a decline of EUR 31 million in Russia, net fee and commission income rose to EUR 1,422 million (first half of 2025: EUR 1,353 million), mainly due to the increase in Hungary, Czechia and at HO. Core earnings therefore rose by EUR 63 million to EUR 4,389 million. Administrative expenses rose from EUR -2,033 million to EUR -2,152 million compared with the same half year period last year. Personnel expenses increased in particular by EUR -83 million due to inflation. Despite a fall in headcount, Russia recorded the largest increase of EUR -36 million, due to currency movements and salary adjustments. Furthermore, higher expenditure on advertising, IT and the transaction tax in Hungary in particular led to an increase in administrative expenses. Impairment losses on financial assets amounted to EUR -111 million in the first half of 2026 (first half of 2025: EUR -109 million). The NPE ratio stood at 1.6% at 30 June 2026 (31 December 2025: 1.7%), while the NPE coverage ratio rose from 46.5% to 49.2% compared with 31 December 2025. The CET 1 ratio was 18.3% at 30 June 2026 (31 December 2025: 17.9%). The carrying amount of the investment in the RBI Group was subjected to a test for a reversal of impairment at the reporting date of 30 June 2026 due to a sharp rise in the share price. The fair value less sales costs as at 30 June 2026 was determined to be EUR 55.85 per share, based on the stock exchange rate of RBI on the Vienna Stock Exchange (31 De-cember 2025: EUR 38.30 per share). The value in use is determined on the basis of an external company valuation. The company valuation was calculated based on the present value of the cash flow to be expected (discounted cash flow procedure) of the companies in the Group taking into account the adjustments required for the purpose of calculating the value in use. Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich analysed the planning assumptions in great detail and made more conservative assumptions regarding the Russian business and the development of the core business compared to the management of RBI and concerning the calculated enterprise value. In order to take into account the effects of the war in Russia and Ukraine, a method based on the dual control approach was used to determine the value in use. The total value of the RBI Group is made up of two components: core business (RBI Group excluding Russia) and the Russian network bank. The effects of possible spin-off and sale options with regard to the Russian subsidiary bank have not been included in the company valuation. The assessment contains three scenar-ios for each of these (Low, Mid and High Case) for both value components (RBI Group excluding Russia and the network bank Russia). In the valuation of the Russian network bank, possible scenarios – ranging from pacification to further escalation – with corresponding probabilities of occurrence and the current restrictions on distributions were also taken into account depending on the further development of the war between Ukraine and Russia. The mid-case scenario rep-resents the expected value of the RBI Group excluding Russia, which is why this scenario was used to calculate the recognised value in use. A conservative weighting of scenarios from the low case was used to determine the value in use of network bank Russia. The discounting of the cash flow that can be achieved with the valuation object was undertaken with the aid of a risk-adequate capitalisation interest rate. For the valuation of the RBI Group excluding Russia, a cost of equity after tax of 9.55% was used (31 December 2025: 9.91%). Any change to capital costs of plus or minus 100 basis points would result in a fall or rise of the established company value of RBI Group by -11.33% or +14.03% respectively. The sustainable growth rate for both value components (RBI Group excluding Russia and the network bank Russia) was set at 2.00% (31 December 2025: 2.00%). The beta factor for the core business was derived from a peer group of internationally active banks with a risk profile comparable to that of RBI but without a significant exposure in Russia. The beta factor for the valuation of the Russian network bank was determined from a peer group of Eastern European local banks. Due in particular to the lower cost of equity and higher earnings forecasts, the value in use improved significantly at 30 June 2026 to EUR 45.90 per share compared with 31 December 2025 (31 December 2025: EUR 37.95 per share). Section 6 (1) no. 28 second sentence UStG exempts other services from VAT that are provided between companies that predominantly carry out banking, in-surance or pension fund transactions, insofar as these services are used directly to carry out the aforementioned tax-free transactions, and for the provision of personnel by these entrepreneurs to the groups mentioned in the first sentence of Section 6 (1) no. 28 UStG. Hedge accounting Fixed interest rate risk positions as part of the ordinary business activities of the Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich Group result from the conclusion of loans and term deposits with customers as well as from the purchase of securities and from issues. These fixed interest rate risk positions are hedged either by means of micro hedge accounting or a portfolio fair value hedge. In micro hedge accounting, mainly positions on the liabilities side are hedged with regard to their fixed interest rate risk in order to reduce negative maturity transformation effects. Furthermore, on the asset side, there is an increase in interest rate hedging on a micro basis for large-volume customer transactions with stable cash flows and in the securities area. With fair value hedge accounting on a portfolio basis (“portfolio fair value hedge”), interest rate risks at the Raiffeisenland-esbank Oberösterreich Group are managed at the level of three dynamic portfolios. Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich Group’s risk management identifies fixed-interest underlying transactions on the basis of defined criteria and allocates them to the relevant hedge portfolio. The underlying transactions represent fixed-interest loans and securities as well as deposits and liabilities evidenced by certificates in euros in the category “At amortised cost” (AC) (fixed-interest asset portfolio and fixed-interest liability port-folio). These transactions also meet other general criteria (e.g. no underlying transactions in a micro hedge, no defaulted or inter-company transactions). Variable interest instruments in which caps and floors are embedded also have a fixed interest rate risk, at least tempo-rarily, if the figures exceed or fall below the interest rate limits (cap/floor portfolio). Variable financial assets with interest rate floors are accounted for in a separate portfolio. Loans, promissory note loans and securities with explicit floors are allocated to this portfolio currently in compliance with the criteria listed above. Sensitivity information on allowances and provisions in Stages 1 and 2 In accordance with IFRS 9, “forward looking information” – meaning macroeconomic forecasts – is used to calculate the balance sheet allowances and provisions. Based on this, statistical models are used to determine the IFRS 9 risk param-eters and subsequently the balance sheet allowances and provisions. Both the macroeconomic forecasts and the calcu-lated risk parameters are subject to estimation uncertainty in the model. In order to be able to better assess and estimate this uncertainty due to changed parameters, the Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich Group calculates sensitivity anal-yses of the balance sheet allowances and provisions in Stages 1 and 2 and presents them on the following pages. At the reporting date 30 June 2026, realisations are in use until 2025 for the macroeconomic factors used. These are no longer affected by an HCPI or real estate price shift and therefore remain unchanged for the sensitivity analysis. The shift to the macroeconomic forecasts will take effect from 2026. HCPI shift of +/–2 percentage points: the HCPI is an important macroeconomic indicator from Raiffeisenlandesbank Ober-österreich’s perspective. It was therefore identified as a relevant metric for the sensitivity analysis. The 2 percentage point shift in the annual HCPI growth rate is used to show the sensitivity to the PD risk parameter. A parallel shift is performed on all annual HCPI forecast values. Based on the changed HCPI growth rates, alternative IFRS 9 PDs are determined, which are subsequently used for staging and for the calculation of the allowances and provisions on the balance sheet per shift scenario. The amount of the shift was chosen on the basis of an expert estimate and represents a mean change in the risk parameters. Changes in parameters were presented as a shift in the GDP growth rate of +/–1 percentage point at 31 December 2025, rather than in the HCPI growth rate. The change was made in response to the growing importance of the harmonised consumer price index. Real estate price shift +/-5% points: The fluctuation of the residential and commercial property price growth rate is the central explanatory factor in the IFRS 9 LGD models of Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich and was therefore identified as a relevant metric for the sensitivity analysis. Specifically, both the current projected residential and commercial property price growth rate per year and the residential and commercial real estate securities are reduced or increased by 5 per-centage points. This results in an indirect shift of the IFRS 9 LGD and thus an increased or reduced balance sheet allow-ances and provisions. Furthermore, the real estate securities for each account are reduced or increased by 5 percentage points in absolute terms for the purposes of the sensitivity analysis. The amount the shifts was chosen on the basis of an expert estimate and represents a mean change in the risk parameters. Principles of risk management The long-term success of Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich Group is largely dependent upon active risk management. In order to achieve this target, Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich, as the dominant group company, has implemented risk management with structures that facilitate the identification and measurement of all risks in the Group in accordance with sections 39, 39a, Austrian Banking Act and the Credit Institution Risk Management Regulation (KI-RMV) (credit risks, equity risks, liquidity risks, market risks, macroeconomic risks, operational risks and other risks) and their active managerial counteraction. Credit, investment and operational risk are managed by RMKM (Risk Management Credit, Reporting, Op-erational Risk), while liquidity, market and macroeconomic risk are managed by RMIM (Risk Management ICAAP & Market Risk). ESG (environment, social, governance) risks, as the latest dimension of risks, were integrated into the existing risk categories, with the greatest focus remaining on climate and environmental risks – in part because social and governance risks have not been classified as material. To this end, inputs in the form of metrics and scores are provided centrally by a unit that is organisationally assigned to RMIM. The Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich in general only aims its work at business areas in which it has the requisite expertise in the assessment of the specific risks. The inclusion of new business areas or products is preceded by an appropriate analysis of the business-specific risks. Risk Controlling analyses all risks and examines adherence to the defined risk limits by means of ongoing variance anal-yses. Internal/Group Audit assesses the effectiveness of working procedures, processes and internal controls. 7.1.2. Integration of climate and environmental risks in risk management Climate and environmental risks form part of the risk inventory of existing risk categories. The relevant risk area is therefore responsible for measurement and reporting - creating the parameters, metrics and resulting analyses that serve as input, as well as the general transfer of expertise, are carried out by a central unit within risk management. The annual risk inventory enables changes in financial materiality to be recognised and, if necessary, measures (e.g. increased monitoring) to be derived. The traditional risk committees are ultimately served automatically by integrating climate and environmental risks into the existing risk categories. Climate and environmental risks are analysed in two dimensions for risk management purposes. These are represented by temporary and physical climate and environmental risks. Accordingly, these dimensions are considered separately. Specific metrics are required in each case here to enable the measurability and therefore the assessment of the different aspects of climate and environmental risks. Transitory climate and environmental risks Transitory climate risk is the term used to describe financial losses that may occur directly or indirectly as a result of adapting to or failing to adapt to a lower-carbon and more environmentally sustainable economy. The transmission channel thus results, for example, from technical progress, changes in market regulations and preferences or the increasing and rising pricing of greenhouse gas emissions. In addition to climate risks, changes in the environment due to external influences can also lead to transitory risks. Com-panies have a strong influence on ecosystem services as part of their own business activities. The risks for companies (and the associated transmission channel) can arise, on the one hand, from regulations but also from taxes and levies (e.g. for water consumption, pollution, land utilisation). Interim Financial Report 2026 87 The Group IFRS consolidated interim financial statements 2026 | Notes to the consolidated financial statements | Risk report The Group Interim Financial Report 2026 | Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements 87 Physical climate and environmental risks Essentially, physical climate risks relate to the more frequent (change in probability) and more intense (level of damage) occurrence of extreme weather events and natural hazards. In order to assess the materiality for the Bank, it is necessary to consider physical risks from two perspectives. On the one hand, physical risks differ geographically based on the pre-dicted change in each region, and the question of “Where is financing provided?” must therefore be clarified. On the other hand, such events can have a strong impact on a wide range of corporate activities. The transmission channel thus results, for example, from additional costs or disruptions to operations (caused by extreme weather events or natural hazards) as well as supply chain bottlenecks or a business model risk. In addition to climate risks, changes in the environment due to external influences can also lead to potential financial risks. Changes in natural capital (e.g. water and soil) can have serious impacts on sectors or businesses that depend on certain ecosystem services. Severely affected sectors or businesses are likely to suffer losses if they cannot access necessary ecosystem services to the extent to which they are accustomed. The transmission channel thus arises from a reduced ecosystem service because the required natural capital is not available in sufficient quantities or not (or no longer) in the required quality. Scenarios and time horizons As part of the risk inventory, different scenarios and time horizons are taken into account when assessing climate and environmental risks by risk type. A materiality assessment was carried out for each scenario and each selected time horizon using standardised matrices (scenarios and time horizons). The risk types use metrics tailored to the dimensions (e.g. scores, simulated PD shifts) as a basis for this, which are then applied qualitatively or quantitatively by the risk types, taking into account the different scenarios and time horizons. The results for each risk type are shown in the tables below. The NGFS scenarios (Network for Greening the Financial System) described below were used as scenarios for climate risks: The “Orderly Transition” scenario is based on the assumption that climate policy actions are introduced at an early stage and tightened on a continuous basis. Both transitory and physical risks are limited in the short term. Over the 2030 and 2040 time horizons, business models that have not invested in decarbonisation will be increasingly faced with higher costs and the resulting consequences. The physical consequences of climate change increase until 2030 due to the early intro-duction and ongoing tightening of climate change mitigation actions, but this acceleration will slow down by 2040 and the consequences will therefore not become more frequent/intensive (compared to 2030). A high transition risk arises in the “Disorderly Transition” scenario due to delayed or different policies in countries and/or sectors. Delayed action e.g. results in a (necessary) abrupt increase in the price of CO2. This in turn puts too much of a strain on many business models that are heavily affected by rising CO2 prices, especially up to 2040, and for which the high price increase is not economically viable. The development of the physical consequences of climate change in the “Disorderly” scenario is, in fact, the same as the one for the “Orderly Transition”. In the “Hothouse World” scenario, it is assumed that climate policy actions will be implemented in some countries, but that global efforts will not be sufficient to stop significant global warming. The consequences of this are increasingly high physical risks over the various time horizons, which have irreversible consequences for society and the economy. Two scenarios are considered with regard to environmental risks, for which an internal elaboration based on the NGFS scenarios was carried out. The “business as usual” scenario assumes that no major (political) efforts are made to protect natural capital. Companies can therefore consume and, in many cases, overconsume, the resources they need, such as water and land. The first impact can therefore be expected by 2030, while many resources will no longer be available in the required form by 2040, resulting in high costs. These in turn mean that some business models will no longer function in their original form. Credit risk The credit risk constitutes the risk to the bank that a loss will occur as a result of the non-fulfilment of the contractual obligations of customers or contracting partners. The credit risk results mainly from loans and advances to customers and banks and from securities from the banking book. Credit risk comprises the following sub-categories: counterparty or credit risk, securitisation risk, concentration risks (con-centration risk relating to individual borrowers, sector distribution, country risk, foreign currency loans and repayment instruments) and CVA risk. Climate and environmental risks are quantified within the credit risk framework using stress scenarios as part of the integrated stress test. Interim Financial Report 2026 90 The Group Interim Financial Report 2026 | Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements 90 Counterparty and credit risks are calculated using the present value approach. The risk is communicated through the key risk figure for “unexpected loss”. For credit ratings higher than 10A, the calculation is carried out using MSCI’s CreditMan-ager programme. The risks and opportunities from loan defaults or changes in creditworthiness are determined using a market valuation model. The risk for default classes 10A to 10C is calculated separately. Unsecured portions of exposures for which no specific provision has been made are allocated to the unexpected loss. An LGD of 67.0% is applied for retail customers, and an LGD of 39.4% for corporate customers (Best Estimation of Expected Loss (BEEL)). The loan portfolio is analysed – broken down by IFRS segments, specific industries, ratings or rating models, NACE sectors and regions – and reported to the Managing Board on a monthly basis. Credit risk concentrations are identified by analysing each borrower or group of borrowers. In addition, the counterparty risk report provides quarterly or ad hoc reporting on credit risk to the Managing Board. For the purposes of the group’s risk reporting, it takes into account all elements of credit risk related to loans and advances, such as individual debtor default risk, country and sector risks. Equity investment risk Equity investment risk refers to the potential risk of a future impairment in the value of equity investments. Equity invest-ment risk comprises several types of sub-risk, some of which are interdependent and are therefore intertwined. The most significant risks in this regard are the risk of dividend default, the risk of current value depreciation, the risk arising from the reduction of hidden reserves, macroeconomic risks at the level of the equity investment (cash flows and capitalisation rates), and the risk arising from industry concentrations. The Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich Group has a broadly diversified equity investment portfolio. A value-at-risk model is used to assess the risk potential from equity investments, which calculates statically significant iterations based on these external expert valuations (generally expert values based on the discounted cash flow) and subsequently deter-mines the corresponding risk potential for the economic perspective (99.9%) by comparing the calculated value-at-risk values (confidence interval: 99.9%) with the expert value for each participating interest. Historical fluctuation intensities observed in the market with regards to cash flow volatilities (of the underlying industry) and discount rates are applied to the input parameters used in the expert valuation procedure; and statistically significant iterations are thus calculated. The procedure is similar for proportional values of listed participations. The risk potential of the entire equity investment portfolio can thus be determined by aggregating the risk potential of all equity investments. Based on the existing external valuations (market capitalisation or appraiser ratings at the end of the relevant financial period), the risk potential from investments is quantified using a simulation model. The spread of the net result from valu-ation of equity investments is determined on the basis of a Monte Carlo simulation depending on fluctuating input factors, in accordance with their historical volatility. The outcome is a distribution of probabilities for the individual equity investment values. This can then be used to determine the potential risk for the equity investments and thus for the entire equity investment portfolio. In addition to qualitative analyses of data quality and model design, the validation of the equity investment risk model includes above all backtesting. This involves checking whether the risk potential forecast by the model adequately covers both book value and market value losses. The operative business activities of the investments are closely monitored by sending members of the board at Raiffeisen-landesbank Oberösterreich to Managing Boards, Supervisory Boards, and other committees. Periodic equity investment risk management includes the analysis and testing of financial statements and planning figures. From the perspective of equity investment risk, geopolitical conflicts (Russia-Ukraine, Middle East), volatilities in relation to US tariff policy and changes in inflation and interest rate expectations posed risks for companies in the investment portfolio throughout 2025. The first half of 2026 was marked by an unexpected shock (the war with Iran). Increased volatility was observed in the cost structure in the case of energy-intensive portfolio companies (AMAG, voestalpine), and the conflict led to growing planning uncertainties. Transitory climate and environmental risks Multiple transitional risks could arise in relation to equity investments along the corresponding value chain (intermediate products, production, end products). This gives rise to financial risks for equity investments as a result of bans on end products, more onerous regulatory requirements or additional taxation for the end consumer, which may make products considerably more expensive (e.g. stricter emissions standards for cars). If these political measures lead to a fall in demand for the (end) products manufac-tured by the equity investment, this will expose the company to corresponding risks. Physical climate and environmental risks Physical risks are financial risks arising directly from the adverse effects of climate and environmental change on the relevant investment. The acute physical vulnerabilities, in the form of natural disasters resulting from global warming (e.g. floods, landslides, etc.), are primarily concentrated in the industrial investments and the real estate sector of the equity investment portfolio. Model for climate and environmental risks in the investment portfolio An overall environmental score (E-score) will be calculated in future for Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich AG’s equity investment portfolio based on the weighted E-scores of the individual equity investments, with the data being supplied by Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich’s contracting parties. The E-Score will be calculated based on the scores provided and a mapping via the NACE allocation to the corresponding participating interests. The respective total score for the entire investment portfolio will result from the exposure-weighted aggregation of the individual scores for each equity investment. In the course of acquiring a new investment, the assessment made by investment risk management is supported as much as possible by due diligence performed by external experts. In addition, the Financing Management unit issues an opinion on the risk assessment of the acquisition object. Interest rate risk management Interest rate risk management at Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich is carried out on the basis of management strate-gies agreed with the Managing Board as a whole and financial targets. The interest rate projections and the respective concerted positioning are continuously presented within the framework of the Asset Liability Committee. At the consoli-dated level, the aim is to achieve a fixed-interest surplus in order to capture maturity transformation outcomes in future. Interest rate risk is managed primarily through underlying transactions (loans, issues) or their hedging. For asset items in proprietary fond holdings, a “statement of financial position review” is carried out; the bonds contained within the fund thus enter into the hedging strategies of the consolidated banking book. Underlying business transactions can be classified as fair value option in order to reduce the statement of financial position fair value risk of the overall position. For this purpose, however, a partial or full hedging transaction must exist for this underlying transaction. It is also possible to link several underlying transactions with one hedging transaction if the busi-ness content is almost identical. An explicit increase in the interest rate risk of the FVPL position by including a transaction in the fair value option is avoided. In addition to hedges at the individual level of Assets and Liabilities in the form of hedge accounting, Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich manages interest rate risks at the macro level within the framework of the application of the “portfolio fair value hedge”. Both fixed-interest assets and liabilities in defined maturity bands are combined into an overall risk position and hedged with corresponding derivative hedging transactions. It should be noted that variable instruments in which caps/floors are embedded also have fixed interest rate risks. The bottom layer approach is applied in accordance with the EU carve-out regulations on IAS 39. Impact on risk-bearing capacity from an economic perspective (99.9%) The objective is to analyse, from an economic point of view, the risk-bearing capacity under stress conditions for all types of risk and the risk coverage and to determine the respective risk utilisation. The calculation of stressed credit risk is carried out by simulating rating downgrades of individual borrowers operating in an industry significant to Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich, which has a strong negative outlook. In addition to the rating downgrade, a reduction in securities is simulated. Moreover, in the area of credit risk, the impact of spread changes on the exposure and the associated risk is taken into account. The stressed equity investment risk is determined using the ROBert simulation tool (Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich Equity Investment Risk Tool) on the basis of stressed input parameters (e.g. cash flow profitability). In the area of market risk, interest rate and credit spread risk are subjected to stress testing. Upon adjusted interest rates and spreads, the present value of the portfolio is recalculated. The change in present value resulting from the interest rate spread shift has a direct impact on the risk covering potential. As part of liquidity risk management, the scenarios defined by the Austrian Raiffeisen Protection Scheme (Öster-reichischen Raiffeisen-Sicherungseinrichtung – ÖRS) “Reputation Crisis”, “Systemic Crisis” and “Problem Case” – are simulated and the resulting refinancing risk is determined. In the case of a reputation crisis, the critical situation is based on damage to the Raiffeisen name or reputation in any form. The resulting consequences are mapped in the reputation crisis model. The systemic crisis scenario reflects a broader market crisis, irrespective of whether Raiffeisen itself is directly affected by a specific crisis situation. The problem case is a combination of the two isolated crisis cases. The modelling largely reflects a combination of these crisis scenarios. In terms of operational risk, the total simulated default amount of the n-largest borrowers and the occurrence of the n-largest loss events can be simulated. Furthermore, it is possible to simulate other scenarios, such as the Iran conflict, a US tariff scenario, the war in Ukraine or the 2008 financial crisis. In addition, scenarios regarding climate and environmental risks are already being integrated into the stress test frame-work. Currently, the focus is on transitory climate risks, which arise primarily from changing political and legal framework conditions. The NGFS scenarios (Orderly, Disorderly, Hot House – 2030, 2040, 2050 respectively) are used as the basis for climate stress tests at Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich. The results of the scenarios are derived from CGE (Com-putable General Equilibrium) modelling, which uses the respective NGFS scenario metrics as shock parameters. The resulting stressed probabilities of default per customer or sector are subsequently used to simulate specific credit risk indicators, such as, for example, for the balance sheet allowances and provisions in accordance with IFRS 9 (expected credit loss), for the 99.9% unexpected loss and for the RWAs. It is also possible to simulate a physical climate risk as well as the loss of the customers with the highest GHG emissions. It is also possible to analyse the impact of defined recovery options. The quantification of the catalogue of measures in the ICAAP is updated annually on the basis of Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich’s recovery plan; the measures are therefore based on the recovery options in the recovery plan. When a climate stress scenario is applied in this context, a rating simulation is carried out based on the NGFS “Orderly Transition 2050” scenario. The scenario is based amongst other things on the CO2 intensity of the business models of Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich’s individual customers and on how a rise in the price of CO2 that accompanies this affects their cost structure and financial covenants, and thereby their credit ratings. ICAAP From an economic perspective within the ICAAP, the NGFS “Orderly Transition 2050” scenario, including physical risks, is taken into account as a deduction from the coverage in the risk-bearing capacity analysis. Furthermore, the other NGFS scenarios and their impact on risk allocation from the economic perspective of the ICAAP are presented as a simulation within the integrated stress test. The NGFS “Orderly Transition 2050” scenario is also taken into account from the ICAAP’s normative perspective. 7.3.2. EBA/SSM SREP stress test The impact on the income statement and on the regulatory capital ratios is also considered within the scope of the EBA or SSM-SREP stress test. The time frame is three years and the stress is implemented in accordance with the methods stipulated by the authority. 7.3.3. Institutional protection scheme Raiffeisen Banking Group Upper Austria The Raiffeisen Banking Group Austria (RBG Ö) is Austria's largest banking group with 264 local Raiffeisen banks, eight regional banks and Raiffeisen Bank International AG in Vienna. Around 1.7 million Austrians are members and thus co-owners of Raiffeisen banks. Raiffeisen Banking Group Upper Austria (RBG OÖ) is made up of a central institution, Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberöster-reich AG, and 66 Raiffeisen banks with a total of 382 bank branches. About 304,600 Upper Austrians are co-owners of the Upper Austrian Raiffeisen banks. As banks within the network of a co-operative society, the Raiffeisen banks are bound to the principles of subsidiarity, solidarity, and regionalism. Aid association of RBG OÖ Raiffeisen Kredit Garantiegesellschaft m.b.H. Together, the Upper Austrian Raiffeisen banks have established a joint aid association with Raiffeisenlandesbank Ober-österreich AG (joint aid association of RBG OÖ and Raiffeisen-Kredit-Garantiegesellschaft m.b.H.), which ensures that in case of economic problems the distressed institutions receive help through adequate measures. Interim Financial Report 2026 113 The Group The Group Interim Financial Report 2026 | Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements 113 Deposit guarantee scheme The new Austrian Deposit Guarantee Scheme and Investor Compensation Act (ESAEG), which implements a European Directive, came into force in 2015. All member institutions of Raiffeisen Banking Group Upper Austria have been joint members of the “Österreichischen Raiffeisen-Sicherungseinrichtung eGen” since 29 November 2021. The act anticipates the establishment of a deposit guarantee fund that is stocked by annual contributions from banks. The target volume achieved in 2024 amounts to 0.8% of covered deposits. If these funds are insufficient in the event of loss, the banks may be required to provide an additional 0.5% of the covered deposits annually. Deposits are secured up to EUR 100,000 per customer per institute. This applies to both natural and legal entities. Not covered are all deposits listed in section 10 (1) of the Austrian Deposit Guarantee Scheme and Investor Compensation Act (ESAEG) (including deposits from financial institutions, investment firms, insurance companies, pension funds and government agencies). Covered deposits must be reimbursed within seven working days of the occurrence of a collateral event. Another guarantor for the security of deposits is the Austria-wide institutional protection scheme (Raiffeisen-IPS), which was newly founded in 2021 and which both Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich and all Upper Austrian Raiffeisen banks have joined. The main focus of attention in this process is on Tier 1 capital. At the same time, the risk-bearing capacity is determined on the basis of regulatory and economic criteria. It is equal to the maximum losses that the bank or the group could incur without falling below the minimum capital requirements.
